To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the rate of cortical growth increases with age, increases as a function geodesic distance, and correlates with changes in diffusion anisotrophy.

the cerebral cortex in the neonatal brain undergoes a rapid growth spurt that is related to the transition from neuronal proliferation and differentiation, that the rate of growth is higher in regions of cortex that are farther from the origin of neurogenesis, and that the rate of cortical growth is positively correlated with the increase in anisotropy in white matter over the same time interval.

the rate of cortical growth is related to the relative geodesic position of the region of interest in the transverse neurogenic gradient and that the relative cortical growth is related in a spatially specific manner to the change in the fractional diffusion anisometry over time.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development and implementation of new methods to quantify the spatial and temporal variations in growth and folding of the cerebral cortical surface.
the mechanisms that control the growth of the cerebral cortex and the development of cortical folds during development.
the mechanisms that drive folding of the cerebral hemispheres during development.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the cortical folding pattern of the ferret brain is similar to humans in terms of cortical thickness, cortical growth, and sulcal patterns, but different in the timing of these events.
the ferret is a suitable animal for the study of cortical development.

the cortical surface area transitions from slow growth (12.7mm2/day) to fast growth (36.6mm2/day) approximately 13days after birth and the relative cortical growth rate is related to the relative geodesic distances from the origin of transverse neurogenative gradient and fractional anisotropy.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the cortical surface area transitions from an early slower to a higher rate approximately 13 days postnatally, which coincides to the time of transition between neuronal proliferation and differentiation.
cortical growth in the developing ferrets is not homogeneous and is related to changes in the underlying tissue.
we have developed a method to study cortical growth in vivo, and we have applied it to a developing mammalian model.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the transition from neuronal proliferation and migration in the cerebral cortex to morphological differentiation and synaptogenesis is associated with a change in the relative rate of cortical growth, which is spatially and temporally variable.
the cortical surface area transitions from slower to faster growth rates at a time when neurons transition from proliferation to differentiation.
cortical growth rate varies as a function of cortical location and that this variation in growth rate is related to the variation in the underlying white matter microstructure.
